script.opening: "Honestly, I don’t know why my daughter’s made such a fuss. I just caught my foot on the carpet — these old rugs, they’re a menace. It’s nothing to do with me being doddery; I’m perfectly capable. I really don’t want a load of people traipsing through my house deciding I can’t cope. Can you just tell her I’m fine so she stops on at me?"

facts.text: If explored beyond "the carpet": three falls in three months — a recurrent faller by definition. The latest she lay on the floor ~40 minutes before help (a long lie — a red flag for serious consequences). Some occurred on standing (possible postural drop). No clear loss of consciousness, but worth excluding syncope/cardiac causes.

A multifactorial cluster: polypharmacy (two antihypertensives incl. a diuretic, amitriptyline — anticholinergic/sedating, zopiclone — sedating/falls-risk), possible postural hypotension, impaired vision (cataracts awaiting surgery), and likely home hazards. Each is modifiable; the meds are the highest-yield.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the minimising is fear: she is terrified that admitting to falls means losing her home and being "put in a home". The blame on the carpet is a shield. Underneath she is frightened by the long lie (she couldn’t get up and thought no one would come), and she has quietly stopped going out, becoming isolated, because she’s scared of falling outside.

If reached: she equates a falls assessment with surveillance and the first step to a care home; the daughter’s worry is the reliable signal. Reframing the assessment as the route to STAYING independent is the key.

Officially: to be told she’s fine so her daughter stops fussing. What is needed: a proper multifactorial falls assessment (meds review/deprescribing, postural BP, vision, gait/balance, bone health, home hazards) framed around preserving independence, with a personal-alarm/long-lie safety net.

ice.ideas: It was just tripping on the carpets — nothing to do with her health; she’s perfectly capable.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror that admitting to falls means losing her home and being "put in a home"; frightened by lying on the floor unable to get up, and quietly isolating herself for fear of falling outside.
ice.expectations: To be reassured and left alone. What she actually needs: a multifactorial falls assessment and medication review framed around keeping her independent, plus a long-lie safety net.

cues: "I just tripped on the carpet" — a single external cause offered to deflect a multifactorial problem; three falls is recurrent.
Lay on the floor 40 minutes — a long lie; a major red flag she’s glossed over.
"I don’t want people deciding I can’t cope" — the fear of losing independence driving the minimisation; the daughter’s worry is the signal.

checkpoints.text: Recognises this as RECURRENT falls (≥2 in a year) warranting a structured MULTIFACTORIAL assessment (NICE NG249: a comprehensive falls assessment for anyone who has fallen in the last year and had 2 or more falls, was injured, lost consciousness or could not get up on their own — she meets three of these; NG249 advises against falls risk prediction tools to decide this), and does not accept "just the carpet" as the explanation

Prioritises the MEDICATION review/deprescribing as highest-yield: two antihypertensives incl. a diuretic (postural drop), amitriptyline (anticholinergic/sedating — rarely justified for sleep at 79) and zopiclone (sedating, falls-risk) — plans rationalisation through a structured medication review (NICE NG249; NICE NG5; the STOPP/START criteria, international, as a prompt), withdrawing amitriptyline gradually rather than abruptly (BNF) and tapering zopiclone if taken regularly

Covers the other multifactorial domains: postural BP face to face (NICE NG136: lying or seated, then after standing for at least 1 minute; a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant, with or without symptoms), U&E (thiazide-related hyponatraemia), an ECG if any fall suggests a blackout, vision (cataracts awaiting surgery — expedite), gait/balance and strength (physio/falls service), continence, cognition, footwear, alcohol, and home-hazard assessment (OT)

Addresses BONE HEALTH and the long lie: a bruised hip and recurrent falls warrant fracture-risk/osteoporosis assessment (NICE NG259: FRAX or QFracture in women aged 65 and over; treat according to NOGG 2024 thresholds; DXA where the result would change management) and a check for a missed fracture if she cannot weight-bear or the hip pain worsens, and the 40-minute long lie is flagged as a red flag (rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, hypothermia, fear) prompting a personal-alarm/lifeline solution
Considers syncope/cardiac causes where relevant (falls on standing, any blackout) and refers to the falls service / appropriate pathway rather than managing piecemeal
Hears the fear beneath the minimisation and the daughter’s worry as the reliable signal; does not collude with "tell her I’m fine"

Reframes EVERY intervention around PRESERVING independence and dignity: a falls assessment and the right changes are how she STAYS in her home, not the road to a care home; partners with her (and, with consent, her daughter)

Safety-nets and coordinates: deprescribe with a plan and BP recheck, falls-service/OT/physio referral, expedite cataract surgery, bone-health assessment, a personal alarm and "fall + can’t get up = 999", and a defined review — risk reduced, independence protected

worked.txt: "I hear you on the carpets — and we should sort those too. But can I be honest with you, Eunice? Three falls in three months usually isn’t just the rugs; it’s often a handful of small things adding up, and the good news is most of them are fixable. I’m not interested in deciding you can’t cope — I’m interested in keeping you on your feet and in your own home."

"The thing that actually worries me most — last time you were on the floor about forty minutes before anyone came. That must have been frightening, lying there wondering if anyone would. That on its own is a reason for us to act, because next time we want help to reach you fast."

"Here’s the most powerful bit, and it’s easy: several of your tablets can make you light-headed or unsteady — the water tablet, the old sleeping one, and the zopiclone. We can safely trim those back, and I’d expect the falls to improve a lot. That’s not taking something away from you; it’s removing things that are tripping you up."

"I think the real worry under all this is that a falls assessment is the first step to a home. Let me turn that right around: it’s the opposite. The whole point — the right tablets, getting your cataracts done sooner, a bit of balance work, a check of the house — is exactly what keeps you independent and OUT of a home. My goal is your front door staying yours."

"Because you bruised your hip and you’ve fallen a few times, I want to check your bone strength too, so a fall doesn’t become a broken hip. And I get the sense you’ve stopped going out for fear of falling — that’s understandable, but it makes you weaker and more isolated, which raises the risk. Let’s build your confidence back with the right support."

"So: I’ll review and adjust your tablets and check your blood pressure lying and standing, get the falls team and an occupational therapist to look at balance and the house, chase your cataract op, and check your bones. And let’s get you a personal alarm — a button you wear — so if you ever go down and can’t get up, help comes quickly; that’s always a 999, never a wait. I’ll ring you in a week. None of this is about taking over — it’s about you staying you, at home."

f.learning: Three falls in three months is recurrent falls requiring a structured MULTIFACTORIAL assessment (NICE NG249: 2 or more falls, injury or being unable to get up each qualifies — she has all three), not acceptance of "just the carpet". The highest-yield intervention is almost always the MEDICATION review/deprescribing — here a polypharmacy cluster (two antihypertensives including a diuretic, amitriptyline, zopiclone) driving postural drop and sedation. The full assessment spans postural BP (NICE NG136: a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more after standing for at least 1 minute is significant), vision (expedite the cataracts), gait/balance/strength (physio/falls service), continence, cognition, footwear, alcohol, home hazards (OT), and — importantly — bone health (a bruised hip + recurrent falls warrants fracture-risk assessment per NICE NG259 and NOGG 2024, with DXA where it would change management) and the long lie (40 minutes on the floor is a red flag prompting a personal alarm). The examinable hidden agenda is the fear that admitting falls means losing her home; the minimisation is a shield and the daughter’s worry is the reliable signal. Reframe every intervention around PRESERVING independence — the assessment is how she STAYS home, not the road to a care home — and safety-net the long lie. Dignity protected, risk reduced.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG249 (2025) · NICE NG5 (2015) · NICE NG259 Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026) · NICE NG136 (updated 2026) · NOGG 2024
knowledge.summary: Three falls in three months with a long lie is not “the carpets”. It needs a comprehensive falls assessment in which the medication review is the highest-yield step, plus bone health and a plan for getting help after a fall — all framed around keeping her at home.

points.h: She qualifies for a full assessment
points.t: NICE NG249: offer a comprehensive falls assessment to people who have fallen in the last year and who are living with frailty, have had 2 or more falls, had an injury needing treatment, lost consciousness, or were unable to get up on their own. She meets at least two of these. NG249 advises against using falls risk prediction tools to decide this.

NICE NG249 and NICE NG5: structured medication review to find medicines that raise falls risk. Here: a diuretic plus amlodipine (postural drop, low sodium), amitriptyline (sedating, anticholinergic, postural hypotension) and zopiclone (sedation, unsteadiness). Withdraw amitriptyline gradually rather than abruptly (BNF), and taper zopiclone if used regularly.

NICE NG136: measure BP lying or seated, then after standing for at least 1 minute; a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant — review medication and measure later readings standing. Falls on standing up make this the key examination, which needs a face-to-face review.

Gait, balance and strength (falls service or physiotherapy), vision (cataracts — ask the eye service about priority), continence and night-time toileting, cognition and mood, feet and footwear, and a home hazard assessment by occupational therapy. Check U&E (thiazide-related hyponatraemia) and consider an ECG if any fall suggests a blackout.

NICE NG259: assess fracture risk (FRAX or QFracture) in women aged 65 and over, and treat according to NOGG 2024 thresholds; DXA where the result would change management. A fall with a bruised hip at 79 must also be checked for a missed fracture if she cannot weight-bear or pain worsens.

Being unable to get up risks pressure damage, dehydration, hypothermia and muscle breakdown, and feeds fear of falling. Offer a personal alarm or telecare, teach how to get up or stay warm, and treat fear of falling (NICE NG249).

dg.d: Open question; accepted the carpet story as part of the history without stopping there; let her set out her worries.
Lives alone, stopped going out, daughter’s role, sleep habits and fear of care-home placement.
Face-to-face lying and standing BP, hip examination, gait and balance; U&E; ECG if blackout suspected; FRAX or QFracture with DXA as indicated.
Postural hypotension from medicines vs sedation vs visual impairment vs syncope vs environmental trip.
Screened for blackout, chest pain and palpitations; checked she can weight-bear; recognised the long lie as a red flag.
Recurrent falls, likely multifactorial: medicine-related postural drop and sedation, impaired vision, fear of falling.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Planned deprescribing with a gradual amitriptyline and zopiclone taper; falls service, OT, bone health, cataract priority and personal alarm.
Indapamide and amlodipine reviewed against standing BP and sodium; fear of falling and isolation addressed.
999 if unable to get up; same-day contact if hip pain worsens; face-to-face review this week; daughter involved with consent.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “woozy after standing”, the 40-minute long lie and “I’ve not been out much since”.
Idea (the carpet), concern (being put in a home), expectation (reassurance to pass to her daughter).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror that admitting to falls means losing her home and being "put in a home"; frightened by lying on the floor unable to get up, and quietly isolating herself for fear of falling outside — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Barley? I’m one of the GPs — thank you for ringing. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Open question, letting her tell it her way

model.text: Honestly, I don’t know why my daughter’s made such a fuss. I caught my foot on the carpet, that’s all. I’m perfectly capable. I don’t want a load of people traipsing through my house deciding I can’t cope. Can you just tell her I’m fine?

I can hear you value your independence, and I want to protect that too. I’m not in the business of deciding people can’t cope. Could we go through the falls together, so I can see if anything is making them more likely? Then we’ll talk about what would actually help.
model.why: Acknowledges her priority and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Well, if we must.
How many times have you fallen in the last few months?
Three, I suppose. Since the summer.
Can you tell me about them — what were you doing just before each one? Were any when you’d just stood up?
model.why: Explores circumstances, including falls on standing

model.text: One was the carpet. The others… I’d got up out of the chair and went a bit woozy, then I was down.
Did you black out at all, or have any chest pain or a racing heart beforehand?
model.why: Screens for syncope and a cardiac cause

model.text: No, nothing like that. Just woozy.
And the last time — how long were you on the floor, and how is the hip now?
model.why: Asks about the long lie and the injury

model.text: About forty minutes. I couldn’t get up. It’s bruised, but I’m walking on it.
Forty minutes on the floor must have been frightening. What went through your mind while you were lying there?
model.why: Names the long lie and invites the emotion

model.text: (quiet) That nobody would come. I’ve not been out much since. I’m scared of going down in the street.

Thank you for telling me that. Can I check your tablets? I have amlodipine and indapamide for blood pressure, amitriptyline for sleep, and zopiclone when you need it. Is that right, and how often do you take the zopiclone?
model.why: Medication reconciliation, focused on falls-risk drugs

model.text: That’s right. The zopiclone when I can’t settle.
And how’s your eyesight, your waterworks at night, your memory, and how much are you drinking day to day?
model.why: Covers vision, continence, cognition and intake

model.text: Eyes are poor — I’m waiting for the cataract operation. Nothing else to speak of. I don’t drink much of anything.
I wonder whether part of the worry about people coming round is what it might lead to. What are you most afraid of?
Being put in a home. Once they decide you can’t cope, that’s it.
That makes complete sense, and I’m glad you said it. Can I tell you what I think is going on, and why I see this differently?

Three falls, two of them when you felt woozy after standing, usually aren’t about the carpet. Some of your tablets can drop your blood pressure when you stand, and the sleeping tablets make people unsteady. The cataracts don’t help. The good news is that these are the fixable parts.
model.why: Explains the multifactorial picture in plain words

model.text: The thing that worries me most is the forty minutes on the floor. Next time, I want help to reach you in minutes, not an hour.
model.why: Flags the long lie as a priority

model.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.
And about the home — this assessment is the opposite of that. Everything I’m suggesting is about keeping your front door yours.
model.why: Reframes the assessment as protecting independence

model.text: Here’s what I’d suggest. I’d like to see you this week to check your blood pressure lying and standing and look at the hip, with a blood test for your salts and kidneys. Then we can start trimming the tablets — the sleeping ones slowly, not all at once. How does that sound?
model.why: Face-to-face assessment and a planned deprescribing

model.text: I’ve had the amitriptyline for years. I won’t sleep.
That’s a fair worry. We’d reduce it gradually and look at other ways to help your sleep, and if it’s not working, we’ll talk again. You stay in charge of the pace.
model.why: Shares the decision and addresses her concern

model.text: I’d also like to refer you to the falls team for balance and strength work, ask an occupational therapist to look at the house, check your bone strength, and ask the eye clinic about your cataract date. And a personal alarm you wear, so help comes quickly.
model.why: Falls service, OT, bone health, cataracts and alarm

model.text: An alarm… I suppose that’s better than lying there. Will you tell my daughter all this?
Only what you’re happy for me to share. It might help to have her there next time — would you like that?
model.why: Respects confidentiality and offers to involve her daughter

model.text: Until I see you: stand up slowly and sit on the bed edge for a moment first. If you fall and can’t get up, or hurt yourself badly, that’s a 999 call — not a wait. And if the hip gets more painful or you can’t put weight on it, ring us the same day. What will you tell your daughter tonight?
That the doctor’s sorting my tablets and getting me an alarm, and it’s to keep me at home.

social.t: Living alone and no longer going out since the long lie. Fear of falling leads to inactivity, weakness and loneliness, which raise falls risk further.
Her daughter prompted the call and is a reliable second source, but Eunice decides what is shared.

legal.t: Presume capacity. She can decline an alarm or a home visit; an unwise decision is not proof of incapacity. Assess capacity only if there is a reason to doubt it for a specific decision.
She can have a local authority needs assessment for equipment, adaptations and support; community alarm and telecare schemes are usually arranged locally.

professional.t: Ask her permission before sharing the plan with her daughter (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Listening to the daughter’s concerns is always allowed.
Structured medication review with shared decisions (NICE NG5); involve the practice pharmacist and document the reason for each change and the taper plan.

community.t: Community falls service and strength-and-balance classes, occupational therapy home hazard assessment, personal alarm or telecare, Age UK for befriending and practical help.

redFlags: Long lie — 40 minutes unable to get up
Bruised hip after a fall at 79 — unable to weight-bear or worsening pain needs same-day assessment for fracture
Any blackout, chest pain or palpitations before a fall — consider cardiac syncope
psychosocial: Lives alone; stopped going out through fear of falling
Daughter worried; fear of losing independence
Sleep habits and reliance on sleeping tablets
ice: Idea: “I just caught my foot on the carpet.”
Concern: being “put in a home” if she admits she is falling
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her daughter stops worrying

playbook.diagnosis: Recurrent falls, likely multifactorial: probable medicine-related postural hypotension (amlodipine, indapamide, amitriptyline), sedation (amitriptyline, zopiclone), impaired vision from cataracts and fear of falling, with a long lie and a soft-tissue hip injury.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “These falls aren’t really about the carpet. Some of your tablets can make your blood pressure dip when you stand up, the sleeping tablets make you unsteady, and your eyes aren’t helping. Those are all things we can change.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that admitting to the falls means losing your home. My aim is the opposite — to keep you on your feet and in your own house.”
management.psychosocial: Build confidence back step by step: falls team exercise, an alarm so she feels safe going out, and her daughter involved only as she wishes.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face this week: lying and standing BP, hip examination, U&E
Gradual taper of amitriptyline and zopiclone; review indapamide and amlodipine against standing BP
Falls service, OT home assessment, FRAX or QFracture with DXA as indicated, cataract priority, personal alarm
safetyNet: Fall and unable to get up, or a serious injury — 999
Worsening hip pain or unable to weight-bear — same-day contact; review within a week

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station tests whether you can see past a plausible single cause and a patient who minimises. Candidates fail by colluding with “the carpet”, by missing the medicines, or by making her feel she is being assessed for a care home.

items.fail: Accepting the carpet as the cause and advising on rugs only.
items.why: Recurrent falls need a comprehensive assessment under NICE NG249; “management not in line with UK best practice”.
items.fix: Ask about each fall, especially the ones after standing up, and say that three falls usually have several causes.

items.fail: Never looking at the medicines, or stopping them all at once.
items.why: The medication review is the highest-yield intervention; abrupt withdrawal of amitriptyline or zopiclone causes rebound and withdrawal symptoms.
items.fix: Name the falls-risk drugs and plan a gradual, agreed taper with a postural BP check.

items.fail: Forgetting the hip, bone health and the long lie.
items.why: A missed fracture or a second long lie is the serious outcome in this case.
items.fix: Check weight-bearing, plan fracture risk assessment, and arrange a personal alarm.

items.fail: Talking about safety at home as if a move is being considered.
items.why: It confirms her fear, and she will hide future falls.
items.fix: Name the fear and reframe: “Everything here is about keeping you in your own home.”

items.fail: Agreeing to report back to her daughter, or ignoring the daughter entirely.
items.why: Either breaches her confidentiality or loses a reliable ally.
items.fix: Ask what she is happy to share and offer to include her daughter next time.

items.fail: Doing the whole plan by phone with no face-to-face review.
items.why: Postural BP and a hip examination cannot be done by telephone; the plan is incomplete.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face review this week and give a specific 999 and same-day safety-net.

Number, circumstances (woozy on standing), blackout, the long lie, the hip, all four falls-risk medicines, vision, continence, cognition, intake.
Isolation since the long lie and the fear of being “put in a home”. Name it before explaining.
Fixable causes, the long-lie priority, face-to-face postural BP, gradual deprescribing, falls team, OT, bone health, cataracts, personal alarm.
Stand slowly; 999 if she can’t get up; same-day if the hip worsens; review this week; teach-back about her daughter.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “the carpet”, suggests a new rug and ends the call; never reviews the medicines; misses the long lie and the hip; tells the daughter “she’s fine” or ignores her; no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Recognises recurrent falls needing a full assessment; identifies the falls-risk medicines and plans a review; arranges postural BP; refers to the falls service; mentions bone health and an alarm; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out the fear of a care home and the isolation, and reframes every step as protecting her independence; plans a gradual, agreed taper of amitriptyline and zopiclone; checks the hip and the long lie properly; offers to involve her daughter with consent; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get those rugs taped down and see how you go.”
avoid.instead: “The rugs are worth sorting, but three falls usually means several small things adding up, and most are fixable.”
avoid.why: Accepting a single external cause misses the medicines and the postural drop.

avoid.dont: “We need to think about whether you’re safe living alone.”
avoid.instead: “Everything I’m suggesting is about keeping you safe in your own home.”
avoid.why: It confirms her worst fear and she will stop reporting falls.

avoid.dont: “Stop the amitriptyline and zopiclone from today.”
avoid.instead: “We’ll bring the sleeping tablets down gradually, at a pace you’re comfortable with.”
avoid.why: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound and withdrawal symptoms, and imposing it loses her agreement.

SCA_MODELS.text: Eyes are poor — I’m waiting for the cataract operation. Nothing else to speak of. I don’t drink much of anything.
I wonder whether part of the worry about people coming round is what it might lead to. What are you most afraid of?
Being put in a home. Once they decide you can’t cope, that’s it.
That makes complete sense, and I’m glad you said it. Can I tell you what I think is going on, and why I see this differently?

Three falls, two of them when you felt woozy after standing, usually aren’t about the carpet. Some of your tablets can drop your blood pressure when you stand, and the sleeping tablets make people unsteady. The cataracts don’t help. The good news is that these are the fixable parts.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the multifactorial picture in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: The thing that worries me most is the forty minutes on the floor. Next time, I want help to reach you in minutes, not an hour.
SCA_MODELS.why: Flags the long lie as a priority

SCA_MODELS.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.
And about the home — this assessment is the opposite of that. Everything I’m suggesting is about keeping your front door yours.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes the assessment as protecting independence

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s what I’d suggest. I’d like to see you this week to check your blood pressure lying and standing and look at the hip, with a blood test for your salts and kidneys. Then we can start trimming the tablets — the sleeping ones slowly, not all at once. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Face-to-face assessment and a planned deprescribing

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve had the amitriptyline for years. I won’t sleep.
That’s a fair worry. We’d reduce it gradually and look at other ways to help your sleep, and if it’s not working, we’ll talk again. You stay in charge of the pace.
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the decision and addresses her concern

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d also like to refer you to the falls team for balance and strength work, ask an occupational therapist to look at the house, check your bone strength, and ask the eye clinic about your cataract date. And a personal alarm you wear, so help comes quickly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Falls service, OT, bone health, cataracts and alarm

SCA_MODELS.text: An alarm… I suppose that’s better than lying there. Will you tell my daughter all this?
Only what you’re happy for me to share. It might help to have her there next time — would you like that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects confidentiality and offers to involve her daughter

SCA_MODELS.text: Until I see you: stand up slowly and sit on the bed edge for a moment first. If you fall and can’t get up, or hurt yourself badly, that’s a 999 call — not a wait. And if the hip gets more painful or you can’t put weight on it, ring us the same day. What will you tell your daughter tonight?
That the doctor’s sorting my tablets and getting me an alarm, and it’s to keep me at home.

SCA_STEM.name: Eunice Barley
meds: Amitriptyline (started some years ago for sleep)
SCA_STEM.recent: Three falls in the last three months; the most recent left a bruised hip and she was on the floor for about 40 minutes before help came. BMI 21. No falls assessment or bone-health assessment on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone appointment. Her daughter asked her to call about the falls.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG249 (2025) · NICE NG5 (2015) · NICE NG259 Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026) · NICE NG136 (updated 2026) · NOGG 2024
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Three falls in three months with a long lie is not “the carpets”. It needs a comprehensive falls assessment in which the medication review is the highest-yield step, plus bone health and a plan for getting help after a fall — all framed around keeping her at home.

points.h: She qualifies for a full assessment
points.t: NICE NG249: offer a comprehensive falls assessment to people who have fallen in the last year and who are living with frailty, have had 2 or more falls, had an injury needing treatment, lost consciousness, or were unable to get up on their own. She meets at least two of these. NG249 advises against using falls risk prediction tools to decide this.

NICE NG249 and NICE NG5: structured medication review to find medicines that raise falls risk. Here: a diuretic plus amlodipine (postural drop, low sodium), amitriptyline (sedating, anticholinergic, postural hypotension) and zopiclone (sedation, unsteadiness). Withdraw amitriptyline gradually rather than abruptly (BNF), and taper zopiclone if used regularly.

NICE NG136: measure BP lying or seated, then after standing for at least 1 minute; a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant — review medication and measure later readings standing. Falls on standing up make this the key examination, which needs a face-to-face review.

Gait, balance and strength (falls service or physiotherapy), vision (cataracts — ask the eye service about priority), continence and night-time toileting, cognition and mood, feet and footwear, and a home hazard assessment by occupational therapy. Check U&E (thiazide-related hyponatraemia) and consider an ECG if any fall suggests a blackout.

NICE NG259: assess fracture risk (FRAX or QFracture) in women aged 65 and over, and treat according to NOGG 2024 thresholds; DXA where the result would change management. A fall with a bruised hip at 79 must also be checked for a missed fracture if she cannot weight-bear or pain worsens.

Being unable to get up risks pressure damage, dehydration, hypothermia and muscle breakdown, and feeds fear of falling. Offer a personal alarm or telecare, teach how to get up or stay warm, and treat fear of falling (NICE NG249).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; accepted the carpet story as part of the history without stopping there; let her set out her worries.
Lives alone, stopped going out, daughter’s role, sleep habits and fear of care-home placement.
Picked up “woozy after standing”, the 40-minute long lie and “I’ve not been out much since”.
Idea (the carpet), concern (being put in a home), expectation (reassurance to pass to her daughter).
Face-to-face lying and standing BP, hip examination, gait and balance; U&E; ECG if blackout suspected; FRAX or QFracture with DXA as indicated.
Postural hypotension from medicines vs sedation vs visual impairment vs syncope vs environmental trip.
Screened for blackout, chest pain and palpitations; checked she can weight-bear; recognised the long lie as a red flag.
Recurrent falls, likely multifactorial: medicine-related postural drop and sedation, impaired vision, fear of falling.
Planned deprescribing with a gradual amitriptyline and zopiclone taper; falls service, OT, bone health, cataract priority and personal alarm.
Indapamide and amlodipine reviewed against standing BP and sodium; fear of falling and isolation addressed.
999 if unable to get up; same-day contact if hip pain worsens; face-to-face review this week; daughter involved with consent.

social.t: Living alone and no longer going out since the long lie. Fear of falling leads to inactivity, weakness and loneliness, which raise falls risk further.
Her daughter prompted the call and is a reliable second source, but Eunice decides what is shared.

legal.t: Presume capacity. She can decline an alarm or a home visit; an unwise decision is not proof of incapacity. Assess capacity only if there is a reason to doubt it for a specific decision.
She can have a local authority needs assessment for equipment, adaptations and support; community alarm and telecare schemes are usually arranged locally.

professional.t: Ask her permission before sharing the plan with her daughter (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Listening to the daughter’s concerns is always allowed.
Structured medication review with shared decisions (NICE NG5); involve the practice pharmacist and document the reason for each change and the taper plan.

community.t: Community falls service and strength-and-balance classes, occupational therapy home hazard assessment, personal alarm or telecare, Age UK for befriending and practical help.

redFlags: Long lie — 40 minutes unable to get up
Bruised hip after a fall at 79 — unable to weight-bear or worsening pain needs same-day assessment for fracture
Any blackout, chest pain or palpitations before a fall — consider cardiac syncope
psychosocial: Lives alone; stopped going out through fear of falling
Daughter worried; fear of losing independence
Sleep habits and reliance on sleeping tablets
ice: Idea: “I just caught my foot on the carpet.”
Concern: being “put in a home” if she admits she is falling
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her daughter stops worrying

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Recurrent falls, likely multifactorial: probable medicine-related postural hypotension (amlodipine, indapamide, amitriptyline), sedation (amitriptyline, zopiclone), impaired vision from cataracts and fear of falling, with a long lie and a soft-tissue hip injury.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “These falls aren’t really about the carpet. Some of your tablets can make your blood pressure dip when you stand up, the sleeping tablets make you unsteady, and your eyes aren’t helping. Those are all things we can change.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that admitting to the falls means losing your home. My aim is the opposite — to keep you on your feet and in your own house.”
management.psychosocial: Build confidence back step by step: falls team exercise, an alarm so she feels safe going out, and her daughter involved only as she wishes.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face this week: lying and standing BP, hip examination, U&E
Gradual taper of amitriptyline and zopiclone; review indapamide and amlodipine against standing BP
Falls service, OT home assessment, FRAX or QFracture with DXA as indicated, cataract priority, personal alarm
safetyNet: Fall and unable to get up, or a serious injury — 999
Worsening hip pain or unable to weight-bear — same-day contact; review within a week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station tests whether you can see past a plausible single cause and a patient who minimises. Candidates fail by colluding with “the carpet”, by missing the medicines, or by making her feel she is being assessed for a care home.

items.fail: Accepting the carpet as the cause and advising on rugs only.
items.why: Recurrent falls need a comprehensive assessment under NICE NG249; “management not in line with UK best practice”.
items.fix: Ask about each fall, especially the ones after standing up, and say that three falls usually have several causes.

items.fail: Never looking at the medicines, or stopping them all at once.
items.why: The medication review is the highest-yield intervention; abrupt withdrawal of amitriptyline or zopiclone causes rebound and withdrawal symptoms.
items.fix: Name the falls-risk drugs and plan a gradual, agreed taper with a postural BP check.

items.fail: Forgetting the hip, bone health and the long lie.
items.why: A missed fracture or a second long lie is the serious outcome in this case.
items.fix: Check weight-bearing, plan fracture risk assessment, and arrange a personal alarm.

items.fail: Talking about safety at home as if a move is being considered.
items.why: It confirms her fear, and she will hide future falls.
items.fix: Name the fear and reframe: “Everything here is about keeping you in your own home.”

items.fail: Agreeing to report back to her daughter, or ignoring the daughter entirely.
items.why: Either breaches her confidentiality or loses a reliable ally.
items.fix: Ask what she is happy to share and offer to include her daughter next time.

items.fail: Doing the whole plan by phone with no face-to-face review.
items.why: Postural BP and a hip examination cannot be done by telephone; the plan is incomplete.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face review this week and give a specific 999 and same-day safety-net.
